CS163 · A guide to your Leo folder

Your ABR code, explained

A map of the project and a line-by-line reading companion to the code you have on disk. Start with the flow, then open a file to see its source beside an explanation.

1 · What are you building?

Your goal is to estimate an auditory brainstem response (ABR) waveform from an EEG recording and the times of the sound pulses. First, a denoising network learns what training ABRs look like. Later, reconstruction combines that learned model with the observed EEG.

Clean training ABRsAdd diffusion noiseTrain network to predict vSave trained weights
EEG + pulse timesStart from noiseEstimate a clean ABRUse EEG to guide itRepeat → estimated ABR

Training and reconstruction are different. During training, the optimizer changes the network weights to improve v prediction. During standalone reconstruction, the loaded weights are frozen; the waveform is adjusted using the network and EEG.

2 · Follow one example through the files

  1. Make examples. data.py creates 256-point synthetic clean ABRs. One model amplitude unit represents 0.1 µV.
  2. Define the noise process. diffusion.py creates the 200-step schedule and turns each clean waveform into a noisy input and known v target.
  3. Build the network. model.py defines MLP, CNN and U-Net options. Each predicts v from a noisy waveform and a timestep.
  4. Train it. train.py compares predicted v with target v, updates weights and saves an EMA checkpoint. Its validation loss is v-prediction MSE.
  5. Reconstruct. dps/reconstruct.py loads the model, starts with random noise, repeatedly estimates a clean ABR, compares its predicted EEG to the observed EEG, and uses that gradient to guide the next sample.
  6. Evaluate. dps/demo.py generates synthetic EEG from a known ABR, reconstructs it and computes ABR RMSE against that reference. dps/run_eeg.py instead accepts a prepared EEG and pulse-train file.

3 · Three measurements that answer different questions

MeasurementComparisonWhy it exists
Training / validation v-MSEPredicted v versus the known v training target.Teaches and evaluates the denoising network; it is not reconstruction RMSE.
EEG guidance lossObserved EEG versus the EEG predicted from the current clean-ABR estimate.Produces a gradient used to steer standalone reconstruction. It is RMS across EEG samples.
Reconstruction RMSEThe final reconstructed ABR versus a known reference ABR.Measures waveform recovery when a reference exists, for example in a simulation.

The current standalone guidance loss does not divide by noise standard deviation. Some historical batched experiments and the separate Phoom code retain their original normalization, so their guidance values and reported results need that context. The noise added in the synthetic demo is used to create simulated EEG; it is not supplied to the standalone loss.

4 · What are all the folders?

Folder / fileWhat it contains
dps/Your standalone reconstruction function and two ways to run it.
experiments/Dataset preparation, experiment runners, Phoom comparisons, reporting, tests and server helpers. Some runners use separate implementations and protocols.
results/Saved reports, figures, tables and selected prediction arrays. These are outputs, not programs that train the network.
runs/Local run data such as checkpoints, logs, training/validation tables and working outputs. Contents differ by run and some large files are not in Git.
docs/reconstruction_guide/A focused HTML tutorial and downloadable equation images for the standalone reconstruction.
README.md and experiments/*.mdWritten run instructions, methods and experiment notes. Read these as documentation rather than executable source.
__pycache__/, .pytest_cache/, .ruff_cache/Temporary Python, test and lint caches.
docs/code_guide/This guide and its builder; the builder is a documentation generator, not part of training or reconstruction.

Common output formats: .pt stores model or training state; .npz stores arrays; .csv stores tables; .json stores settings or metadata; .png, .pdf and .svg are figures. The phoom/ implementation lives outside Leo/; some experiment scripts import it.

Useful reports: reconstruction-focused report · Phoom pilot report · visual comparison · detailed reconstruction tutorial.

5 · How to use the code reader

Select a file below to expand it. Each row pairs a line from the actual source snapshot with a reading note. Blank lines are omitted; original line numbers are kept. The seven core Python files have detailed scientific explanations. The remaining experiment, test, shell and configuration files have shorter reading hints: multi-line expressions must be read together, and an automatically generated hint is not a full explanation of every scientific choice.

Suggested order: data.py → diffusion.py → model.py → train.py → dps/reconstruct.py → dps/demo.py → dps/run_eeg.py.

Search filters by filename. Select a filename below, or scroll down and expand a file. The source is a snapshot taken when this guide was built. If a core file changes, the builder requires its detailed line notes to be reviewed before it can be rebuilt.

Defines the 200-step noise schedule, training targets, and conversion from predicted v to a clean estimate.

LineYour codeWhat this line does
1"""Cosine noise schedule and the v-prediction training formulas."""Documentation text describing this file, function, or class.
3import mathImport the named module or objects so this file can use them.
5import torchImport the named module or objects so this file can use them.
8DIFFUSION_STEPS = 200The standard schedule contains 200 diffusion steps.
11def cosine_schedule(steps=DIFFUSION_STEPS):Create the preselected cosine schedule; this is not inferred from an EEG recording.
12 time = torch.arange(steps + 1, dtype=torch.float64) / stepsCreate equally spaced points from the beginning to the end of the schedule.
13 signal = torch.cos(((time + 0.008) / 1.008) * math.pi / 2) ** 2Evaluate the cosine-squared curve describing retained signal.
14 beta = (1 - signal[1:] / signal[:-1]).clamp(max=0.999)Convert neighboring curve values into per-step forward noise variances and cap them for stability.
15 return torch.cumprod(1 - beta, dim=0).float()Multiply the per-step signal-retention factors to obtain cumulative alpha_bar values.
18def make_training_pair(clean, timesteps, noise, alpha_bar):Create a noisy input and the known v target for training.
19 signal_weight = alpha_bar[timesteps, None].sqrt()For each example, compute the square root of its cumulative signal coefficient.
20 noise_weight = (1 - alpha_bar[timesteps, None]).sqrt()Compute the corresponding coefficient for the generated diffusion noise.
21 noisy = signal_weight * clean + noise_weight * noiseMix each clean ABR with generated noise at its sampled timestep.
22 target_v = signal_weight * noise - noise_weight * cleanCompute the v target from the same clean ABR and noise. The model learns to predict this.
23 return noisy, target_vReturn both the noisy model input and its known target.
26def clean_from_v(noisy, predicted_v, timesteps, alpha_bar):Turn the network’s v prediction and noisy waveform into a clean-waveform estimate.
27 signal_weight = alpha_bar[timesteps, None].sqrt()Get the signal coefficient for the requested timestep.
28 noise_weight = (1 - alpha_bar[timesteps, None]).sqrt()Get the noise coefficient for the requested timestep.
29 return signal_weight * noisy - noise_weight * predicted_vApply the v-parameterization identity. An imperfect v prediction gives an imperfect clean estimate.

15def stimulus_matrix(pulses, response_length=WAVEFORM_LENGTH, onset_index=50):Define a matrix that converts one candidate ABR into the EEG predicted from the pulse timings.
16 """Use the pulse timings to turn one ABR into an EEG signal."""Documentation text describing this file, function, or class.
17 pulses = torch.as_tensor(pulses, dtype=torch.float32)Convert pulse weights to a 32-bit tensor.
18 if pulses.ndim != 1 or len(pulses) == 0:Check that pulses is a nonempty one-dimensional sequence.
19 raise ValueError("pulses must be a nonempty one-dimensional array")Stop with a useful error if pulse data are invalid.
20 # Our ABR starts 50 samples before the pulse, so keep that offset here.Code author’s comment: Our ABR starts 50 samples before the pulse, so keep that offset here.
21 eeg_times = torch.arange(len(pulses))[:, None]Make a column of EEG sample indices, one row for each recorded sample.
22 abr_times = torch.arange(response_length)[None, :] - onset_indexMake a row of ABR offsets; sample 50 is aligned to each pulse onset.
23 indices = eeg_times - abr_timesFor each EEG sample and ABR point, calculate which pulse index contributes.
24 valid = (indices >= 0) & (indices < len(pulses))Mark only pulse indices that fall inside the recording.
25 return pulses[indices.clamp(0, len(pulses) - 1)] * validLook up pulse weights and zero out invalid indices. The result is an EEG-length by 256 matrix.
28def load_model(checkpoint_path):Load a previously trained model checkpoint for reconstruction.
29 checkpoint = torch.load(checkpoint_path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)Read the checkpoint onto the CPU using the weights-only loader.
30 model = make_model(checkpoint.get("architecture", "mlp"))Create the recorded architecture; old checkpoints default to the MLP.
31 model.load_state_dict(checkpoint["model"])Load the saved trained weights into the model.
32 model.eval()Switch the network to evaluation mode.
33 for parameter in model.parameters():Visit each network parameter.
34 parameter.requires_grad_(False)Freeze its weights. Reconstruction needs gradients with respect to current, not weight updates.
35 return modelReturn the ready-to-use network.
38def reconstruct(model, eeg, pulses, *, guidance=0.1, seed=1):Reconstruct one ABR from a model, observed EEG, and pulse train. Guidance and seed are keyword arguments.
39 """Start with some noise and use the EEG to guide the ABR reconstructionDocumentation text describing this file, function, or class.
41 EEG must be in the model's amplitude unit.Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
42 The pulse train contains event weights, not EEG voltages.Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
43 """Documentation string; this text describes the surrounding file or function.
44 if guidance < 0:Require a nonnegative guidance strength.
45 raise ValueError("guidance must be nonnegative")Stop this path by raising an error: ValueError('guidance must be nonnegative').
46 eeg = torch.as_tensor(eeg, dtype=torch.float32)Convert the observed EEG to a 32-bit tensor in model amplitude units.
47 matrix = stimulus_matrix(pulses)Build the forward matrix that maps a candidate ABR to predicted EEG.
48 if eeg.ndim != 1 or len(eeg) != len(matrix):Check that the EEG is one-dimensional and has the same length as the pulse train.
49 raise ValueError("eeg and pulses must be 1D arrays of the same length")Stop this path by raising an error: ValueError('eeg and pulses must be 1D arrays of the same length').
50 alpha_bar = cosine_schedule()Build the same kind of 200-step noise schedule used by this model.
51 generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)Create a seeded generator for repeatable random sampling.
52 current = torch.randn((1, WAVEFORM_LENGTH), generator=generator)Start with a random 256-point noisy waveform; it is not an EEG recording.
54 for t in range(len(alpha_bar) - 1, -1, -1):Loop backward through the 200 diffusion timesteps, from 199 to 0.
55 current = current.detach().requires_grad_(True)Forget the previous step’s computation history and enable a fresh gradient with respect to current.
56 step = torch.tensor([t], dtype=torch.long)Package t as an integer tensor so the network knows the current noise level.
57 predicted_v = model(current, step)Use the trained network to predict v for this noisy waveform and timestep.
58 clean = clean_from_v(current, predicted_v, step, alpha_bar)Combine current and predicted v to estimate the clean ABR.
59 predicted_eeg = matrix @ clean[0]Apply the pulse matrix to the estimated clean ABR to predict the recording.
61 # See how well this ABR explains the EEG, then get a direction to fix itCode author’s comment: See how well this ABR explains the EEG, then get a direction to fix it
62 residual = eeg - predicted_eegSubtract predicted EEG from observed EEG, sample by sample.
63 loss = torch.linalg.vector_norm(residual) / np.sqrt(len(eeg))Compute the RMS EEG residual. This standalone loss does not divide by noise standard deviation.
64 gradient = torch.autograd.grad(loss, current)[0]Differentiate the EEG loss through the clean estimate and model with respect to the current noisy waveform.
66 # Take one step towards less noise and nudge it using the EEG.Code author’s comment: Take one step towards less noise and nudge it using the EEG.
67 a = alpha_bar[t]Read the cumulative diffusion-schedule value at the current timestep.
68 previous_a = alpha_bar[t - 1] if t > 0 else torch.tensor(1.0)Read the value for the next cleaner step; use 1 at the clean endpoint.
69 alpha = a / previous_aConvert the neighboring cumulative values into the per-step signal-retention factor.
70 beta = 1 - alphaCompute the corresponding forward-step diffusion-noise variance.
71 mean = (previous_a.sqrt() * beta / (1 - a)) * cleanStart the reverse-diffusion mean with the schedule-weighted clean estimate.
72 mean = mean + (alpha.sqrt() * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)) * currentAdd the schedule-weighted current noisy waveform to that mean.
73 variance = beta * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)Calculate the variance for random sampling of the next diffusion state.
74 noise = torch.randn(current.shape, generator=generator) if t > 0 else 0Draw seeded Gaussian diffusion noise, except at the final step where it is zero.
75 current = mean + variance.sqrt() * noise - guidance * gradientCombine the diffusion mean, scheduled randomness, and the negative EEG-gradient correction.
77 return current.detach().numpy()[0]Detach the final result, convert it to a NumPy array, and remove the batch dimension.

95</style></head><body><main><header><div class="eyebrow">CS163 · A guide to your code</div><h1>How my ABR reconstruction works</h1><p class="lead">A step-by-step guide to <code>Leo/dps/reconstruct.py</code>: what goes in, how the model and EEG work together, and what each loss actually measures.</p><p><a href="equation_pngs.zip">Download all equation PNGs</a></p></header>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
96<section><h2>Start with the goal</h2><p>Given an EEG recording and the times at which sound pulses occurred, estimate the small auditory brainstem response (ABR) that each pulse produced. The code assumes one shared ABR shape and adds the responses from all pulses together.</p>$E01<div class="flow"><span>Known pulses + EEG</span><span>Start with random noise</span><span>Model proposes an ABR</span><span>EEG guides the estimate</span><span>Repeat → reconstructed ABR</span></div><p>The ε in this first equation represents EEG measurement noise. The model has learned what ABR-like waveforms look like. The EEG-guidance term checks whether a proposed waveform also explains this recording.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
97<section><h2>1 · Inputs and output</h2><pre><code>reconstruct(model, eeg, pulses, *, guidance=0.1, seed=1)</code></pre><table><tr><th>Input</th><th>Meaning in this function</th></tr><tr><td><code>model</code></td><td>A trained v-prediction network. <code>load_model()</code> sets evaluation mode and freezes its weights.</td></tr><tr><td><code>eeg</code></td><td>A one-dimensional recording of N samples, in the model’s amplitude units.</td></tr><tr><td><code>pulses</code></td><td>N event weights marking stimulus times. These are event weights, not EEG voltages.</td></tr><tr><td><code>guidance</code></td><td>The strength of the EEG-based adjustment. The default is 0.1.</td></tr><tr><td><code>seed</code></td><td>Controls random draws, so a run can be repeated.</td></tr></table><p>The function returns one 256-sample estimated ABR in model units. In this project, one model unit corresponds to 0.1 µV; <code>run_eeg.py</code> divides EEG by 0.1 before reconstruction and multiplies the output by 0.1 to obtain µV.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
98<section><h2>2 · The stimulus matrix: ABR → predicted EEG</h2><p><code>stimulus_matrix(pulses)</code> builds a matrix <strong>M</strong> with N rows and 256 columns. Each column shifts the pulse train to represent one point of a candidate ABR. Multiplying M by an ABR adds up responses at every pulse time, including overlaps.</p><pre><code>matrix = stimulus_matrix(pulses)Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
99predicted_eeg = matrix @ clean[0]</code></pre><p><code>clean</code> has shape <code>(1, 256)</code>; <code>clean[0]</code> selects its waveform. The result has N samples, matching <code>eeg</code>. Index 50 of the ABR corresponds to stimulus onset: at 10,000 samples per second, the first 50 samples cover 5 ms before onset. The matrix masks shifts that would fall outside the recording.</p><p class="note"><strong>Model assumption:</strong> each pulse produces the same waveform and overlapping responses add linearly. Whether that is adequate for a real recording is a scientific question.</p></section>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
100<section><h2>3 · Why the network predicts “v”</h2><p>During training, the experiment knows a reference waveform <strong>h₀</strong> and adds generated Gaussian noise <strong>ε</strong>. This diffusion noise is separate from the EEG measurement noise in the first equation. At diffusion step t, the schedule <code>alpha_bar</code> determines the mixture:</p>$E02<p>The model’s target is another combination of the same waveform and noise:</p>$E03<p>The network receives the noisy waveform and t, and predicts <code>v</code>. Its weights are learned beforehand; they are not updated during reconstruction.</p><h3>What <code>clean_from_v</code> does</h3><p>Given the noisy waveform and predicted v, the following identity estimates the clean waveform. It would recover the training waveform exactly if v were predicted exactly; in practice it is an estimate.</p>$E04<pre><code>predicted_v = model(current, step)Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
101clean = clean_from_v(current, predicted_v, step, alpha_bar)</code></pre><p>Here, <code>current</code> is hₜ and <code>clean</code> is the estimate ĥ₀. The helper’s implementation is <code>signal_weight * noisy - noise_weight * predicted_v</code>.</p></section>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
102<section><h2>4 · Initialization</h2><pre><code>alpha_bar = cosine_schedule()Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
103generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
104current = torch.randn((1, WAVEFORM_LENGTH), generator=generator)</code></pre><p>The schedule has 200 diffusion steps. The reconstruction starts as random noise, not as an EEG waveform. The seed controls this initial noise and the additional diffusion noise drawn later.</p></section>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
105<section><h2>5 · The loop, one step at a time</h2><p>The loop counts backward from t = 199 to t = 0. Each pass makes a candidate clean ABR, checks it against the EEG, and computes the next waveform.</p><h3>5.1 · Track how the current waveform affects the result</h3><pre><code>current = current.detach().requires_grad_(True)Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
106step = torch.tensor([t], dtype=torch.long)</code></pre><p><code>detach()</code> separates the current iteration from earlier calculation histories. <code>requires_grad_(True)</code> lets PyTorch calculate how the current waveform affects this iteration’s mismatch. With a model obtained from <code>load_model()</code>, its parameters are frozen. The reconstruction function itself performs no optimizer update, even if a caller passes an unfrozen model.</p><h3>5.2 · Estimate a clean ABR</h3><pre><code>predicted_v = model(current, step)Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
107clean = clean_from_v(current, predicted_v, step, alpha_bar)</code></pre><p>The model uses t to know the current noise level. The helper applies the clean-estimate equation above.</p><h3>5.3 · Predict the recording and measure its mismatch</h3><pre><code>predicted_eeg = matrix @ clean[0]Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
108residual = eeg - predicted_eegPass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
109loss = torch.linalg.vector_norm(residual) / np.sqrt(len(eeg))</code></pre>$E05<p>Here y is the observed EEG, M is the stimulus matrix, and N is the number of EEG samples. The result is the <strong>root mean square of the EEG residual</strong>. It measures how well the candidate explains the recording; it is not the reconstruction RMSE against a known ABR.</p><h3>5.4 · Get the guidance direction</h3><pre><code>gradient = torch.autograd.grad(loss, current)[0]</code></pre>$E06<p>PyTorch differentiates through the predicted EEG, clean estimate, and network back to <code>current</code>. The gradient points toward increasing mismatch; the update subtracts it to nudge the waveform toward a lower mismatch.</p><h3>5.5 · What are we trying to do next?</h3>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
110<p>At the start of this block, <code>current</code> is the noisy ABR waveform at step <em>t</em>, <code>clean</code> is the network’s estimate of the final clean ABR, and <code>gradient</code> tells us how the EEG mismatch changes with <code>current</code>. Each is a waveform with 256 values. The loop moves backward from <em>t</em> = 199 toward 0, making a new <code>current</code> at each step.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
111<div class="flow"><span>Current noisy waveform</span><span>Calculate a cleaner diffusion step</span><span>Add scheduled randomness</span><span>Nudge using the EEG</span></div>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
112<p>Here is the entire block. The explanations below follow its lines in order:</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
113<pre><code>a = alpha_bar[t]Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
114previous_a = alpha_bar[t - 1] if t &gt; 0 else torch.tensor(1.0)Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
115alpha = a / previous_aPass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
116beta = 1 - alphaPass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
117mean = (previous_a.sqrt() * beta / (1 - a)) * cleanPass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
118mean = mean + (alpha.sqrt() * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)) * currentPass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
119variance = beta * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
120noise = torch.randn(current.shape, generator=generator) if t &gt; 0 else 0Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
121current = mean + variance.sqrt() * noise - guidance * gradient</code></pre>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
122<h3>5.6 · Look up the current and next noise levels</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
123<pre><code>a = alpha_bar[t]Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
124previous_a = alpha_bar[t - 1] if t &gt; 0 else torch.tensor(1.0)</code></pre>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
125<p><code>alpha_bar</code> is a precomputed schedule describing how much of the original signal is retained after forward diffusion. In the noising equation in section 3, the clean waveform is multiplied by the square root of this value, and the noise by the square root of one minus this value. Values near 1 correspond to less noise; values near 0 correspond to more noise.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
126<p><code>a</code> is the schedule value at the current step <em>t</em>. <code>previous_a</code> is the value at <em>t</em> − 1: the next, cleaner stage during reconstruction. At <em>t</em> = 0 there is no earlier array entry, so the code uses 1 to represent the clean endpoint.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
127<h3>5.7 · Find the coefficients for this one step</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
128<pre><code>alpha = a / previous_aContinues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
129beta = 1 - alpha</code></pre>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
130$E07Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
131<p><code>a</code> and <code>previous_a</code> are cumulative schedule values. Their ratio, <code>alpha</code>, describes signal retention for the single transition between these two stages; <code>beta</code> describes the corresponding forward-step noise variance. The code uses them to calculate the reverse step.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
132<h3>5.8 · Find the center of the next step</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
133<pre><code>mean = (previous_a.sqrt() * beta / (1 - a)) * cleanContinues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
134mean = mean + (alpha.sqrt() * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)) * current</code></pre>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
135$E08Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
136<p>Read the two lines together as <code>mean = clean_weight * clean + current_weight * current</code>. The weights come from the noise schedule. The first line takes part of the network’s predicted clean ABR; the second adds part of the current noisy waveform. They are calculated for every step and applied to every waveform point.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
137<p><code>mean</code> is a 256-point waveform, not one average number. It is the center of the reverse-diffusion distribution: the default next waveform before the random and EEG-guidance terms are added. The network’s <code>clean</code> is an estimate, so it need not be the true ABR.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
138<h3>5.9 · Set the random part</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
139<pre><code>variance = beta * (1 - previous_a) / (1 - a)Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
140noise = torch.randn(current.shape, generator=generator) if t &gt; 0 else 0</code></pre>Pass or define the named value as part of the expression above.
141$E09Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
142<p><code>variance</code> controls how widely the next sample can vary around <code>mean</code>. For <em>t</em> &gt; 0, <code>torch.randn</code> draws Gaussian noise with one value for each point of the waveform. A fixed seed makes these draws reproducible. At <em>t</em> = 0, the code draws no new noise and sets this term to zero.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
143<h3>5.10 · Combine denoising, randomness, and EEG guidance</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
144<pre><code>current = mean + variance.sqrt() * noise - guidance * gradient</code></pre>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
145$E10Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
146<table><tr><th>Term</th><th>What it does</th></tr><tr><td><code>mean</code></td><td>Provides the center of the next, cleaner diffusion step.</td></tr><tr><td><code>variance.sqrt() * noise</code></td><td>Adds random variation at the scheduled scale. The square root converts variance to the standard deviation used to scale Gaussian noise.</td></tr><tr><td><code>- guidance * gradient</code></td><td>Uses the EEG mismatch to nudge the waveform. The gradient points locally toward increasing the loss with respect to <code>current</code>; subtracting it points toward decreasing that loss.</td></tr></table>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
147<p>These terms act on all 256 waveform values. The gradient was calculated through the predicted EEG, <code>clean</code>, and the network back to the old <code>current</code>. It is combined with the diffusion step; because the mean and random term also move the waveform, the EEG loss is not guaranteed to decrease at every iteration.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
148<p>λ is <code>guidance</code>. If guidance is zero, the EEG does not steer the output. Larger values strengthen the correction; in this implementation the correction is not multiplied by the diffusion variance. Choose guidance on separate validation data. To reproduce an earlier update for a fixed recording, divide the old guidance value by the old noise SD in model units.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
149<h3>5.11 · A worked example for one waveform point</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
150<p>These are illustrative values, not measured results. In a real iteration the same schedule coefficients apply to all waveform points, while the clean estimate, current value, noise and gradient vary by point. Suppose <code>a = 0.60</code>, <code>previous_a = 0.75</code>, <code>clean = 0.80</code>, <code>current = 0.40</code>, <code>noise = -0.20</code>, <code>gradient = 0.10</code> and <code>guidance = 0.20</code>. Then:</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
151<table><tr><th>Calculation</th><th>Approximate result</th></tr><tr><td><code>alpha = 0.60 / 0.75</code>; <code>beta = 1 - alpha</code></td><td>0.80 and 0.20</td></tr><tr><td><code>mean = 0.433 * 0.80 + 0.559 * 0.40</code></td><td>0.570</td></tr><tr><td><code>variance = 0.20 * (1 - 0.75) / (1 - 0.60)</code></td><td>0.125</td></tr><tr><td><code>new current = 0.570 + sqrt(0.125) * (-0.20) - 0.20 * 0.10</code></td><td>0.479</td></tr></table>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
152<p>In this example the diffusion mean moves the point from 0.40 to about 0.570; the random term subtracts about 0.071, and the EEG-guidance term subtracts 0.020. The model and the EEG are therefore both involved in the next value.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
153<h3>5.12 · The last step</h3>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
154<p>At <em>t</em> = 0, <code>previous_a = 1</code>. Substituting that value makes <code>mean = clean</code> and <code>variance = 0</code>. No new random noise is drawn, so the last update simplifies to:</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
155<pre><code>current = clean - guidance * gradient</code></pre>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
156<p>After this last correction, the function returns <code>current.detach().numpy()[0]</code> as the estimated ABR. The model weights are not trained or changed by this loop.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
157<section><h2>6 · Three different errors</h2><table><tr><th>Quantity</th><th>What is compared?</th><th>Purpose</th></tr><tr><td>Training v-MSE</td><td>Predicted v vs the known training target v</td><td>Train and validate the network’s diffusion prediction.</td></tr><tr><td>Guidance loss</td><td>Observed EEG vs EEG predicted by the current ABR estimate; RMS across EEG samples</td><td>Calculate the gradient that steers each reconstruction step.</td></tr><tr><td>Reconstruction RMSE</td><td>Final reconstructed ABR vs a known reference ABR</td><td>Evaluate recovery in a simulation or other setting with a reference.</td></tr></table>$E11<p>For real EEG the true ABR is generally unknown, so this exact reference-based RMSE is not directly available. The simulated experiments start from a known reference, use it to generate noisy EEG, reconstruct, then calculate this error. If the reference and reconstruction are in model units, multiply the RMSE by 0.1 to report µV.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
158<section><h2>7 · One sample versus many</h2><p>This particular <code>reconstruct()</code> call returns <strong>one</strong> sample. Repeating it with different seeds can produce different waveforms. An experiment may average several samples before calculating RMSE, or calculate RMSE for each sample and average those errors. Those are different measurements.</p><p>The separate batched experiment code runs the same kind of guidance calculation for multiple observations. The existing batched experiment implementations still use their original noise-normalized loss, so their historical results are unchanged. Later experiments may also apply a covariance-based correction after averaging; that correction is not part of this function.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.

342<style>body{{max-width:1200px;margin:48px auto;padding:0 26px;background:#f8fafc;color:#243247;font:16px/1.65 system-ui}}h1{{font-size:38px;line-height:1.15;color:#0f172a}}h2{{color:#0f172a}}section{{background:white;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:12px;padding:26px;margin:24px 0}}img{{width:100%;height:auto}}table{{border-collapse:collapse;font-size:12px;width:100%}}td,th{{padding:8px;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0;text-align:left}}pre{{white-space:pre-wrap;font-size:12px}}a{{color:#2463a0}}</style>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
343<h1>Reconstruction improvements to Phoom’s DPS recipe</h1><p>Matched-budget pilot · validation-only selection · independent holdout</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
344<section><h2>Protocol and primary outcome</h2><p>The primary metric is mean per-waveform RMSE in µV between a known analytic ABR and the reconstructed mean of 32 stochastic DPS draws. Training v-MSE is a separate diagnostic. Both architectures use exactly Phoom’s synthetic waveform generator, 20,000 training waveforms (seed 5000), dataset-standard-deviation normalization, batch size 256, AdamW at 2×10⁻⁴, zero weight decay, 500-update warmup, and gradient clipping at norm 1. The MLP is Phoom’s 544,768-parameter model; the CNN is Leo’s 7,745-parameter dilated residual network. The single training seed is 0. CNN convolutions use an equivalent explicit-window/GEMM implementation to avoid slow deterministic cuDNN kernels on the GTX 1080; forward outputs and input/parameter gradients are checked against the original convolutions. This is a runtime optimization, not a change in architecture or an RMSE intervention. Equal updates and presentations do not mean equal FLOPs.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
345<p>EMA 0.001 is Phoom’s baseline; EMA 0.005 comes from Leo’s experiments. Both shadows follow the same trained weights, so this ablation requires no extra training. At updates 1,000, 2,000 and {config["steps"]}, validation reconstruction error selects a checkpoint and EMA using eight-draw means. A fixed guidance grid then selects one value per known noise SD. A covariance-regularized correction is tuned on validation recordings, with strength zero explicitly included. The correction solves (I + τ C MᵀM/σ²)h = h_DPS + τ C Mᵀy/σ² using covariance C estimated from training ABRs. It reuses measurements and is an empirically tuned refinement, not an exact posterior update or calibrated uncertainty method.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
346<p>Validation: six nonzero reference ABRs (waveform seed 90422, noise seed 2000). Original benchmark: 12 nonzero reference ABRs (90421, 1000). Fresh holdout: 12 nonzero references (90423, 3000). All observations are half-second recordings with regular 10 ms pulse intervals and white Gaussian noise at SD 0.05, 0.20 and 0.50 µV. All choices are frozen before either test set is scored. Every method shares recordings and Monte Carlo seeds. The original baseline uses the last checkpoint, EMA 0.001 and Phoom’s fixed MLP guidance [10, 31.62, 100]. The selected_fixed variants isolate checkpoint/EMA selection; tuned adds guidance selection; tuned_refined adds the correction.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
347<p>The Gram-statistic implementation accelerates the EEG residual while preserving the same mathematical loss and gradients; a numerical test compares its returned samples with Phoom’s original direct EEG implementation. The code makes no claim that these simulations establish performance on real EEG.</p><p><a href="https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/abr-deconv/{PROJECT}">CoreWeave Forge project</a></p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
348<section><h2>Results</h2><ul>{"".join("<li>" + html.escape(x) + "</li>" for x in findings)}</ul><table><tr><th>Split</th><th>Method</th><th>0.05 µV noise</th><th>0.20 µV noise</th><th>0.50 µV noise</th><th>Mean RMSE</th><th>Reduction vs baseline</th></tr>{"".join(table)}</table></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
349{"".join(blocks)}Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
350<section><h2>Interpretation and limitations</h2><p>This controlled comparison concerns newly trained, matched-budget models. Phoom’s hosted runs include models trained for millions of updates; their checkpoints were unavailable in the repository and Forge artifacts when this experiment began. Logged metrics from those runs are reference observations, not a controlled head-to-head result. A reduction versus the new baseline does not establish superiority over those mature models. The published benchmark has already been inspected by previous work, so the fresh holdout is the stronger check on transfer.</p><p>One training seed and 12 held-out synthetic reference waveforms per set are a pilot, not a population study. Validation selection uses eight draws while final evaluation uses 32; this sampling-budget difference can alter rankings. All waveforms come from the same synthetic generator, which limits physiological generalization. Guidance-grid boundary selections do not identify a global optimum. Averaging and refinement can suppress peaks; RMSE should be interpreted alongside waveform shape and timing. All failures and regressions remain in the tables.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
351<section><h2>Frozen selections</h2><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(choices, indent=2))}</pre><h2>Reproduction</h2><p>From phoom/, run <code>python ../Leo/experiments/phoom_improvements.py</code> in the configured environment. Raw per-record errors, sample arrays, training histories, validation grids and checkpoints are retained. Seven figures are exported as PNG, PDF and SVG; this HTML embeds all plots for standalone viewing.</p><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(config, indent=2))}</pre><h2>Hosted reference runs (not a paired comparison)</h2><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(published, indent=2))}</pre></section></html>"""Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.

236 doc = f"""<!doctype html><html lang="en"><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Longer MLP reconstruction training</title><style>body{{max-width:1150px;margin:48px auto;padding:0 26px;background:#f8fafc;color:#243247;font:16px/1.65 system-ui}}h1{{font-size:38px;line-height:1.15}}section{{background:white;padding:26px;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:12px;margin:24px 0}}img{{width:100%}}table{{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:13px}}td,th{{padding:9px;text-align:left;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0}}pre{{white-space:pre-wrap;font-size:12px}}</style>Store the result of f'<!doctype html><html lang="en"><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Longer MLP reconstruction training</title><st… in doc.
237<h1>Does the reconstruction improvement persist with longer training?</h1><section><h2>Methodology</h2><p>The same 544,768-parameter MLP is trained from seed 0 for {config["steps"]:,} optimizer updates with batch size 256 on 20,000 analytic waveforms. Two EMA shadows, 0.001 and 0.005, follow the same parameter trajectory. Starting from the same seed reproduces the short-budget recipe; prior checkpoints lacked raw optimizer state, so this is a fresh full trajectory, not a claimed optimizer continuation.</p><p>AdamW uses learning rate 2×10⁻⁴, a 500-update warmup, zero weight decay and gradient clipping at norm 1. Waveforms use Phoom’s generator and training-standard-deviation normalization. Reconstruction uses the same 200-step DPS algorithm, with numerically verified Gram-statistic acceleration. The primary outcome is mean per-waveform ABR reconstruction RMSE in µV after averaging 32 stochastic draws, distinct from training v-MSE.</p><p>Checkpoints are assessed on six new validation reference waveforms with eight-draw means. Validation selects checkpoint/EMA, guidance per noise level and covariance-regularized measurement correction. The original benchmark is a previously observed reference, not a new test. The fresh holdout uses new waveform/noise seeds {config["fresh_waveform_seed"]} and {config["fresh_noise_seed"]}, disjoint from the earlier pilot. Each test set has 12 nonzero reference ABRs and half-second recordings with regular pulses every 10 ms and white noise at SD 0.05, 0.20 and 0.50 µV. Settings are frozen before scoring. All methods share measurements and Monte Carlo seeds.</p><p>The correction uses covariance estimated only from training waveforms and includes strength zero as a candidate. It is an empirical reuse of the measurements, not an exact posterior update. There is one training seed; this synthetic study does not establish performance on real EEG. An EMA benefit in a short run need not persist after convergence. {config["steps"]:,} updates are longer than the pilot but do not establish equivalence to Phoom’s million-update models.</p><p><a href="https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/abr-deconv/{project}">CoreWeave Forge project</a></p></section><section><h2>Results</h2><ul>{"".join("<li>" + html.escape(x) + "</li>" for x in findings)}</ul><table><tr><th>Split</th><th>Method</th><th>Mean reconstruction RMSE (µV)</th><th>Reduction vs final slow EMA</th></tr>{"".join(table)}</table></section>{"".join(blocks)}<section><h2>Frozen selections</h2><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(choices, indent=2))}</pre><h2>Protocol</h2><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(config, indent=2))}</pre><p>Raw tables, samples, checkpoints, source hashes and optimizer/RNG resume state are retained beside this standalone report. All figures are exported separately as PNG, PDF and SVG.</p></section></html>"""Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.

382 document = f"""<!doctype html><html lang="en"><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>ABR reconstruction: what improved?</title><style>body{{max-width:1120px;margin:50px auto;padding:0 24px;background:#f2f6f8;color:#17283f;font:16px/1.65 system-ui}}h1{{font-size:clamp(2.2rem,5vw,3.4rem);line-height:1.1;letter-spacing:-.03em}}h2{{color:#17283f}}section,.intro{{background:white;border:1px solid #dce5ec;border-radius:14px;padding:26px;margin:22px 0}}img{{display:block;width:100%;height:auto}}p{{max-width:92ch}}.tag{{color:#007f78;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.14em;font-size:.78rem;font-weight:700}}a{{color:#215d9c}}@media(max-width:650px){{body{{margin:24px auto;padding:0 12px}}section,.intro{{padding:18px}}}}</style><div class="tag">CS163 · reconstruction experiments</div><h1>What improved in ABR reconstruction?</h1><div class="intro"><p>The figures show the completed 4,000-update and 50,000-update Phoom-style MLP experiments. We compare reconstruction RMSE against known reference ABRs, after averaging 32 stochastic reconstructions. Lower RMSE means the reconstructed waveform is closer to its reference.</p><p>At 4,000 updates, faster EMA plus a validation-selected measurement correction reduced mean RMSE by {100 * (1 - new[1] / base[1]):.1f}% on a fresh synthetic holdout. The longer follow-up shows why checkpoint and EMA choices need continued testing.</p><p><strong>Scope:</strong> one training seed; 12 synthetic reference ABRs per test set; half-second EEG simulations with white noise. The Phoom-style baseline is our matched-budget reproduction, not Phoom’s unavailable million-update checkpoint. The ongoing 10-million-update run is not included in these completed results.</p><p><a href="https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/abr-deconv/abr-deconv-phoom-improvements">Open the experiment runs in CoreWeave Forge</a></p></div>{"".join(blocks)}<section><h2>Method and data</h2><p>Both methods share a trained MLP, simulated pulse timings, EEG recordings, and sampling seeds. The baseline uses EMA 0.001 and Phoom’s fixed guidance. The improved pipeline selects EMA/checkpoint and a covariance-regularized EEG correction using validation recordings. The correction reuses the EEG; it is an empirical refinement, not an exact posterior update. Test data are used only for the displayed evaluations.</p><p>The 4k and 50k follow-ups use different fresh holdout seeds. Validation points average eight reconstructions; final test points average 32 before calculating RMSE. Comparisons with Phoom’s actual million-update models require his weights and a shared evaluation. PNG, PDF and SVG exports and the source tables accompany this self-contained page.</p></section></html>"""Store the result of f'<!doctype html><html lang="en"><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, i… in document.

406<div class="eyebrow">CS163 · Caltech · Reconstruction study</div><h1>Recovering ABRs from simulated noisy EEG</h1><p>Evaluated configurations: <strong>{len(models)} / 4</strong> · Two priors, two training seeds</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
407<div class="intro"><h2>Question and design</h2><p>Can a trained diffusion prior recover a reference ABR from a known pulse train and simulated noisy recording? The primary outcome is mean per-observation waveform reconstruction RMSE, not v-prediction error. For each reconstruction: RMSE = sqrt(mean((estimated ABR − reference ABR)²)) × 0.1 µV per model unit.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
408<p>New CNN models are trained independently on analytic waveforms and EARNDB template augmentations, with two training seeds. Each uses 60,000 available training waveforms, batch size 32, AdamW, EMA, and 1,000 optimizer updates. Checkpoints at 200, 400, 800 and 1,000 are assessed with guidance 0, 0.3, 1 and 3 on validation cases. The checkpoint/guidance pair with minimum validation RMSE is frozen before test evaluation. Three sampling seeds assess stochastic sensitivity. A six-value ridge grid is tuned on the same validation observations.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
409<p>The architecture is held fixed: a 7,745-parameter temporal CNN with 16 channels and six residual convolution blocks at dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. Training predicts v using mean squared error under a 200-step cosine diffusion schedule. AdamW uses learning rate 2×10⁻⁴ and weight decay 10⁻⁴, gradients are clipped at norm 1, and EMA uses rate 0.005. Examples are sampled with replacement: 1,000 updates at batch size 32 means 32,000 waveform presentations, not 1,000 epochs.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
410<p>Analytic ABRs vary peak timing, width and amplitude, include a trough and optional early component, and are filtered at 80–1,500 Hz; 10% are null waveforms. EARNDB ABR averages are restricted to SPL≥70 dB and ABR channels identified by nV headers. Digital waveforms have DC removed using the epoch tail, are resampled from 48 to 10 kHz, and are normalized to synthetic 0.04 µV RMS. The periodic epoch tail supplies the negative-time portion of the window; it is not measured pre-onset EEG. Template augmentation uses log-normal gain (log SD 0.2) and shifts from −0.3 to +0.3 ms with zero padding. No test subject contributes to these training templates.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
411<p>EARNDB subjects N1–N5 train the prior, N6 provides validation references, and N7–N8 provide test references. Four reference targets per domain are used in validation and eight per domain in testing (four references each from N7 and N8); each has white/colored noise at synthetic 0.05/0.20 µV standard deviation, giving 32 validation observations and 64 test observations. Analytic targets use independent split seeds. All methods share paired recordings. Observation duration is 0.2 seconds. RMSE is computed over 256 waveform samples, then averaged over observations and sampling seeds. Repeated noisy observations and seeds are not independent subjects.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
412<p>Forward model: EEG = stimulus matrix × reference ABR + noise. Diffusion sampling uses 200 reverse steps and an EEG-residual gradient. The clean reference is excluded from that gradient. Trace RMSE measures the estimated clean ABR at each step; final test RMSE measures the returned reconstruction.</p>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
413<p><a href="https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/abr-deconv/abr-deconv-reconstruction">CoreWeave Forge: training, validation reconstruction and sampling traces</a></p></div>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
414<section><h2>Results</h2><p>{findings}</p><table><tr><th>Training configuration</th><th>Selected update</th><th>Guidance</th><th>Validation RMSE (µV)</th><th>Test RMSE (µV)</th></tr>{bodyrows}</table><h2>Key findings</h2><ul>{finding_items}</ul><h2>Individual held-out participants</h2><table><tr><th>Configuration</th><th>Subject</th><th>ABR RMSE (µV)</th></tr>{subject_table}</table></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
415{"".join(blocks)}Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
416<section><h2>Interpretation and limits</h2><p>This is a small reconstruction-focused pilot. Only one EARNDB participant supplies validation targets and two supply a balanced set of test targets; the number of waveforms does not establish population-level certainty. Template references are measured averages with residual noise and are normalized to synthetic 0.04 µV RMS. Their physical calibration is unresolved. Results measure recovery of those references in simulated EEG, not performance on real continuous EEG. No probability intervals or significance claims are made.</p><p>The early training budget tests checkpoint selection, not maximum attainable performance. Guidance-grid boundary minima should motivate a separately specified validation sweep. A lower denoising loss need not imply lower reconstruction RMSE, and a lower EEG residual need not imply a more accurate ABR. The high-noise waveform examples illustrate that lower average RMSE can coexist with attenuated response peaks. RMSE alone does not establish faithful peak amplitude or timing; the raw test tables also provide waveform correlation and a descriptive 3–10 ms peak-timing error, which is not a validated clinical wave-V annotation. Future improvements should be selected on validation data; repeated test inspection can bias subsequent comparisons.</p></section>Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.
417<section><h2>Reproduction and provenance</h2><p>EARNDB v1.0.0: <a href="https://physionet.org/content/earndb/1.0.0/">PhysioNet dataset</a>, ODC Attribution license. Silva &amp; Epstein (2010), Estimating loudness growth from tone-burst evoked responses, JASA 127:3629–3642, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1121/1.3397457">doi:10.1121/1.3397457</a>. Downloaded record hashes are preserved in the data manifest.</p><p>Run <code>.venv/bin/python experiments/reconstruction_suite.py</code> from Leo. The complete settings are below; source hashes are saved in source_sha256.json. The matching execution sources are preserved in execution_source.zip; the cleaned source tree additionally includes formatting and reporting updates. Raw tables, predictions and checkpoint files remain in the run folder. Separate PNG, PDF and SVG figures are exported under figures/. This report embeds every plot and is readable as a single standalone file.</p><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(config, indent=2))}</pre><h3>Execution environment</h3><pre>{html.escape(json.dumps(environment, indent=2))}</pre></section></html>"""Continues the expression, arguments, documentation, or command begun above; read it together with the surrounding lines.

A note about the experiments

Several experiment runners deliberately preserve the implementation used when their results were recorded. In particular, a batched experiment’s noise scaling, data generation, model architecture, or selection procedure may differ from the standalone reconstruction. A simulated reference is known because it was used to construct the synthetic EEG; real EEG generally does not provide that exact ground truth.

This is an offline HTML document with the code embedded. The companion builder is docs/code_guide/build_code_guide.py; it creates this reading guide and is not needed to train or reconstruct.
